newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonian PM says to quit, sparks crisis.
newsitem.headline: Estonian PM says to quit, sparks crisis.

text.p: Estonian Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi said on Wednesday he will resign, sparking a fresh political crisis in the small Baltic state.
Vaehi, leading Estonia's sixth government since the country quit the former Soviet Union in 1991, said he would quit as soon as a new government was formed.
Vaehi's position had become untenable after he only narrowly won a parliamentary no-confidence vote on Monday.
The veteran politician, who came to power in April 1995, has already been through two political crises and currently leads a minority administration.
"Under the present balance of political powers, there is no point for me to continue as prime minister," Vaehi said in a statement.

"I have decided to step down as prime minister as soon as political parties have agreed on forming a new government enjoying parliamentary support and have also found a candidate for prime minister," he added.
He said he was making the statement to make it clear he wanted to resign.
He said that a statement on Tuesday, in which he said that he would launch talks to form a more solid government, had been misinterpreted as meaning he wanted to hang on to power.
Vaehi first came to power on a wave of public discontent over radical free-market reforms and scandals under a previous right-wing government.
Despite fears he would slow down reforms, Vaehi has pushed ahead with privatisation and made Estonia one of the best economic performers of the former Soviet Union.
Vaehi's current government enjoys the firm support of 41 members of the 101-seat parliament and around five or six independent deputies.
He only narrowly survived the no-confidence vote, with 45 MPs backing it and 46 deputies supporting Vaehi.
Opposition politicians did not see big changes in the ruling parties after Vaehi's announcement.
"Vaehi's statement does not solve the government crisis," Toivo Jurgenson, head of the political faction of the opposition Fatherland Union told Estonian Radio.

"I believe the current coalition will stay together and will just try to regroup. I do not see the possibility at the moment that the present opposition will be involved in forming a new government," he added.
